HW 2: Your first brms model

Due: Thursday, Feb 4 at 2:30 pm on Canvas · Size: full analysis · Points: 20 · Covers: Regression part 1

Start from the homework template, use ## Q1 to ## Q6 headings, and turn in both the .qmd and the rendered .html. Save your brms fits with file = so re-rendering doesn’t refit every time.

Data. Use your own data: one continuous outcome and one continuous predictor. If you don’t have data you can use yet, use sat.act from the {psych} package (verbal SAT, SATV, predicted by ACT) and say so.

library(psych)
d <- sat.act

Q1. Set up the model (2 points)

  1. Describe your outcome and predictor in a sentence each: what they measure, their units, and their range.
  2. Center your predictor, so the intercept means something.
  3. Write the model in likelihood notation, including priors, like we did in class. (Fill in the priors after Q2.)

\[ \begin{aligned} y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\ \mu_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_i - \bar{x}) \\ \beta_0 &\sim \ ? \\ \beta_1 &\sim \ ? \\ \sigma &\sim \ ? \end{aligned} \]

Q2. Priors and the prior predictive (4 points)

  1. Choose a prior for the intercept, the slope, and σ. For each, give one sentence of justification in the units of your variables. For example, “the average SAT verbal score is surely between 400 and 800” is a justification; “normal(0, 10) is weakly informative” is not.
  2. Simulate 100 regression lines from your priors (by hand like in class, or with sample_prior = "only" in brm()) and plot them over the range of your predictor.
  3. Do the lines make predictions that are impossible or absurd for your outcome? If so, revise your priors, show the new prior predictive, and say what you changed. If not, say how you know.

Q3. Fit it two ways (3 points)

  1. Fit the model with lm().
  2. Fit the model with brm() using your priors from Q2.
  3. Put the intercept and slope estimates (and their uncertainty: SE and CI from lm, posterior SD and 95% interval from brms) side by side in a small table. Are they similar? Why would you expect them to be (or not to be) with your data?

Q4. The posterior of your slope (4 points)

  1. Plot the posterior distribution of the slope with {tidybayes} (e.g., spread_draws() and stat_halfeye()).
  2. Add your prior for the slope to the same plot. How much did the data move you?
  3. Summarize the slope with mean_qi(), median_qi(), and mode_hdi(), at both 89% and 95%. Do the point estimates or intervals differ? Why or why not? (Hint: what would make them differ?)
  4. In one or two sentences that a reader of your paper would understand, what does the slope tell you?

Q5. Draws (3 points)

  1. How many posterior draws does your brms model have? Where does that number come from? (Look at chains, iter, and warmup.)
  2. Refit with four times as many draws. What changes in your Q4 summaries, and what doesn’t? Does asking for more draws give you more information about the slope?

Q6. Does the model reproduce your data? (4 points)

  1. Run pp_check() on your brms model (try a couple of type = options, e.g., "dens_overlay" and "stat").
  2. Describe where the simulated data match your observed data and where they don’t. What feature of your data is the model missing, if any? (Bounded scales, skew, and ceiling effects are common culprits.) You don’t need to fix it, just diagnose it.
TipUnder the hood: your model in Stan (optional, not graded)

brms doesn’t fit models itself: it writes a program in Stan, the language that does the sampling, and runs it. You can see that program with stancode(your_model). Take five minutes and find:

  1. The blocks: data, parameters, transformed parameters, model, and generated quantities. What goes in each one?
  2. Your three priors. brms collects them as lines like lprior += normal_lpdf(b | 0, 20);. Do they match what you chose in Q2?
  3. Your likelihood. It’s in the model block, behind if (!prior_only) (that switch is how sample_prior = "only" works!).
  4. The transformed data block quietly centers your predictor, and generated quantities converts the intercept back. That’s why the summary says Intercept but the draws are called b_Intercept.

Nothing to turn in. Later in the semester you’ll write a small Stan program yourself, and this will look familiar.
